It follows from these facts that he was guilty of conspiracy with these men to get from the government or the people of Canada the money that was paid to the men while they were working at his house. It follows further that that money was obtained from the people of Canada through this government by false pretenses of Mr. Lanctot and Mr. Page. Now, is that so? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries would tell you that he consented to the payment of this $375, believing the pay-sheets that were sent to him from Sorel, representing that these men during these five months were working on government work. So that the minister was deceived and the money was obtained from the government by false pretenses. Therefore, I say that the hon. member for Richelieu was a party to defrauding the government; he was one of the conspirators for getting the money from the government; he was a party to getting that money from the government by false pretenses. And that is not all; he induced them to take from the government storehouse in St. Joseph de Sorel to his house on George street, in the city of Sorel, some $80 worth of goods belonging to the government of this country. Now, those goods were not loaned. You cannot borrow a thing unless you return that identical thing. There was no intention of returning the thing. The property in it passed forever from the owners, the people of Canada or the government, to Mr. Lanctot's house. In this connection, I want to read a sentence or two from the third edition of James Crankshaw on the Criminal Code of Canada. At page 413, in considering the section of the code which was read by my hon. friend from St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), section 347, he says:
Theft defined.-Theft or stealing is the act of fraudulently and without colour of right taking, or fraudulently and without colour of right converting to the use of any person, anything capable of being stolen, with intent,-
(a)	to deprive the owner, or any person having any special property or interest there-

in, temporarily, or absolutely, of such thing, or of such property or interest; or, _
(b)	to pledge the same or deposit it as security ; or,
(c)	to part with it under a condition as to its return which the person parting with it may be unable to perform; or,
(d)	to deal with it in such a manner that it cannot be restored in the condition at which it was at the time of its taking and conversion.
And so by putting the paint and putty on Mr. Lanctot's house, they dealt with them so that they could not return them, and there is no evidence that there was any intention of returning the identical goods that they got from the government storehouse.
2.	Theft is committed when the offender moves the thing or causes it to move or to be moved, or begins to cause it to become movable, with intent to steal it.
So that as soon as these goods were taken from the government storehouse the offence was complete.
3.	The taking or conversion may be fraudulent, although effected without secrecy or attempt at concealment.
4.	It is immaterial whether the thing converted was taken for the purpose of conversion, or w'hether it was, at the time of the conversion, in the lawful possession of the person converting.
In commenting upon this section, at page 413, the learned author speaks as follows:
It is generally laid down that any act whicli is an interference with the dominion and right of property of another is a conversion. A conversion does not mean a destruction of the goods nor does it necessarily import an acquisition of property by the defendant or n total or absolute loss of the goods to the owner, but it consists in any wrongful act by which the defendant deprives the owner of his goods either wholly or for a time. To constitute a fraudulent conversion, the owner must be deprived of his property or money bv an adverse using or holding.
Under the terms of section 347, theft by conversion is committed whenever a person,, already in possession of a specific article of personal property with the owner's consent, fraudulently and without colour of right converts it to his own use or to the use cf any other person than the owner of it, with intent to deprive the owner of it, either temporarily or absolutely, or with intent to deprive any person having any special property or interest therein, temporarily or absolutely, of such special property or interest, or with intent to pledge the same or to part with it under a condition, as to its return, which he may not be able to perform, or to so deal with it that it cannot he restored.
This was what the Act dealt with because in this case it was impossible to return the goods.
The effect of section 347 is to put all persons whomsoever, whether they are or are not clerks, servants, employees, hankers, merchants, brokers, solicitors, factors, agents or bailees, upon the same footing, and to make every person whomsoever, without any distinction, guilty of theft by conversion (or what may, perhaps, he more properly termed embezzlement), when, having become rightfully possessed of something belonging to another, he, instead of handing it over, in specie or instead of doing with it what he was entrusted to do, fraudulently and without colour of right, converts it to his own use or to the use of any other person than the owner. In other words, embezzlement by clerks, servants or other employees, fraudulent conversion by bankers, merchants, brokers, solicitors, factors or other agents, of property entrusted to them for safe custody, &c., and larceny by bailees, are three only of the various ways of committing the offence of theft by conversion treated of by section 347. So that it may not be out of place to briefly review some of the authorities on these three subjects.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in taking these goods belonging to the people of Canada from an inferior officer who had no authority to give them the hon. member for Richelieu was strictly within the terms of section 347, of the Criminal Code and was therefore guilty of theft. What is the difference between the position occupied by Mr. Lanctot with reference to these goods and that of a man who goes to an inferior officer in a bank-the teller or the ledger keeper and get $1,000 from him saying to him: I will return this money in a week? The teller or ledger keeper had no authority to give him $1,000, he gives him $1,000, he invests that in margins, at the end of the week the $1,000 is not paid and the clerk is arrested and convicted of embezzlement or theft. The intention of both parties was to return the money at the end of a week or at the end of a month. Why, our prisons are full of men who have embezzled thousands and scores of thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars intending all the time to return the money. I remember that a short time ago a man from our city stole $287,000 before "being arrested, embezzled it, intending every moment to return it as soon as her made it, but he kept on losing and losing, hoping against hope until finally the whole matter was disclosed and he was sent to penitentiary for twelve years. He did not intend to cheat anybody, he intended to return the money just as this man, admit that if you like, intended to return these material's. He did not borrow these goods, but he got these goods promising to return a similar quantity and a like quality of goods just as the young man who gets $1,000 from a bank intends to return, not that identical $1,000, but a like sum of money in ten or thirty days as the case may be. He fails to do it and he is guilty

Now, I desire to say that I was led to an expectation as to the manner in which the charges against the hon. member for Richelieu would be dealt with having read the evidence elicited in the Public Accounts Committee in the charge made against the hon. member for Grenville. We have theTe a case of the hon. member (Mr. Reid, Grenville) who was then, as now, a member of the House seeking to get a favour from the government. I am going to admit at once that the hon. member for Grenville paid the bill when he knew what was due. I will admit that the hon. member might perhaps have been deceived when the caulkers were put to work upon his vessel as to being still upon the pay-roll of the government.

I object there. The caulkers ' the hon. gentleman speaks of were two men who had never before been in the employ of the government. They were brought from Kingston, where they were the employees of Davis & Sons. They were brought down just to caulk three boats, and the minute they were through they were discharged, and ceased to be government employees.

I am merely stating what I read from the evidence. It may have been

a mistake to continue their names on the government pay-roll.
They were never on the government pay-roll for caulking government Boats prior to being on my boat.

I do not desire to enter into a wordy controversy with the hon. member with respect to it. I read the evidence taken from the Public Accounts Committee and which will appear upon the ' Hansard ' to-morrow. The evidence is available, and any one who desires can read it. With regard to the repairs made uipon the boat, and the painting upon the boat of the hon. member for Grenville, the same thing applies. The hon. member, I presume, paid for it when it came to his notice that their time had been charged against the government.
There was never any account presented' to me.

Then it is not paid yet, so it is all the worse for the hon. gentleman. The hon. member for Richelieu desired the use of some men to do work upon his house. He went to the person having charge of these men, who consented that they should go and work upon his house. The time was kept in the same manner in which it was kept in the case of the hon. member for Grenville, and when the work was all done the bill was presented to the hon. member for Richelieu, and he paid the bill, in the same way the member for Grenville would have paid the bill had it been presented to him. Now, with regard to the paint that the member for Richelieu borrowed from the employees of the government at Sorel, the situation is exactly the same as in the case of the hon. member for Grenville. in borrowing the acetylene gas and borrowing the engine, with this difference, that there is no testimony that the member for Grenville ever paid the value of the acetylene ga? or the rent of the engine. The member for Grenville said that -he needed an engine for some special work in his factory, he could not get another one anywhere else, and he went to the Superintendent of the Marine and- Fisheries Department in the town of Prescott, he borrowed an engine, and used it as long as he had any use for it, and then returned the engine to the government. I submit that is the exact set of circumstances in respect to the hon. member for Richelieu. It is true, as the Minister of Justice pointed out, that the member for Richelieu did not return the paint in specie, but he returned it in kind. The person who had control of paints in Sorel swears that he kept an absolutely correct account of the material, and after 252
the work was done he made out a bill for the .material, he gave it to the time-keeper, who handed it over to Mr. Papineau, and the moment the member for Richelieu ascertained the value of the material that bad been used in his house, he gave instructions to have it purchased from the same manufacturer, and he paid the bill, thereby returning to the department at Sorel every penny's worth of material that had been loaned to him. Now, I submit that the circumstances surrounding the transaction in which the hon. member for Grenville was connected are on all fours with the charges made against the member for Richelieu. The member for Richelieu got men from the Department of Marine and Fisheries to do work for him, for which he paid. The hon. member for Grenville, in equal good faith, I presume, got men from the Department of Marine and Fisheries at Prescott, to do work for him, and I am free to admit that if he did not pay for it, it was not his fault, but he would have paid for it if the bill had been rendered to him. Now, there was no hon. member in this House who stood up in his -place in 1908, and charged that the hon. member for Grenville had been guilty of fraud, perjury and malversation, in his dealings with the government in the circumstances I have detailed. If the member for Grenville feels that he has not violated the spirit or the letter of the Independence of Parliament Act, and if hon. gentlemen surrounding him on the opposition side of the House feel convinced that the member for Grenville did not violate the Independence of Parliament Act, then I ask them, in all fairness and in .all honour, how they can ask this House to censure the member for Richelieu in like circumstances. Taking the argument used by hon. gentlemen on the opposition side that were addressed to you, Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, and talcing particularly the arguments used bv the member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), and the member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers), every censure and every condemnation addressed by them tq the member for Richelieu, might apply with equal force and weight, against the member for Grenville, and I think it would put their casuistry and their talent for making fine distinctions to a severe test to convince you that while the member for Grenville has not violated the Independence of Parliament Act and has done nothing for which he should be censured, the member for Richelieu has done something for which he should be censured and condemned under the same circumstances.

which the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has made concerning myself. I cannot conceive that any hon. member of this House, if he had read the evidence as he should have, would have got up and made the statements the hon. gentleman has made about me here to-night. He has produced the evidence, as he states, in this case, and the hon. member admits that he did not read the evidence, he only read part of the evidence.
I read the statements that were germane to the. case.

When I asked the hon. member to read the balance of the evidence he said that he couldn't do it, that he hadn't it. It is not here now, he has only got the one sheet of the evidence. Mr. Noble is one of the leading officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department, he was stationed at Prescott at the time, and was living there every day, and the hon. member, if he read Mr. Noble's statement, would see that he denied absolutely the statements made by the hon. member for Richmond. Mr. Noble stated that he had never heard anything about these repairs until it was brought up at that committee. Now, let me state how this thing happened. The hon. member read my evidence, and I denied the whole of the affair, and there was nothing to prove that my evidence was different. Let me tell the House now how this little matter of mine happened to come up. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is here now, we are face to face and we had better have it out. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that at that time there were investigations going on in the Public Accounts Committee concerning his department. We all know that there were very serious charges against the Marine and Fisheries Department, The minister was up there defending the department, as he should. We had charges there so serious that if the people of this country knew of them, I do not believe they would tolerate this government for one minute. What did the Minister of Marine and Fisheries do in that case? He sent his private secretary out to Prescott and kept him there a week or two as a private detective, to see if he could not find some evidence. After a week or two he got two of these witnesses, the evidence of one of whom the hon. member was reading. He is a man whose oath would not be taken in any part of Prescott or in any other part of Canada, a man who, was himself kept out of jail by his friends. That is one of the men, and the minister has him there yet. Both are men whom you can buy for $10 at any time. But when you get to Mr. Noble, a man of honour, he denied the whole thing. he never heard of it. The caulkers spoken of were not regular government officials, they were only there for two or three weeks, they were brought there from Davis & Sons, of Kingston, and after they were dismissed and were returning to Davis Bros. I had two men for one day each, or $6, and I paid that to Mr. Noble because he paid the men, as they were going away. I never heard of anything being done on my yacht, and I believe that not one dollar's worth of work was put on it; had there been anything put on it, I am sure the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, with the venom he had against me, would have produced the evidence. I defy the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to say that he ever produced an account or rendered an account to me; he never rendered an account, and the account that man swore to was something like one gallon of paint, a few pounds of nails, something like $3.80. Then they charged me, in order to bring up a fraudulent account, with part of the ways -that were built some years before and which are there yet, for which any man knows I would not be expected to pay anything. That was charged up to make a fraudulent account. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries knows that I was in the Public Accounts Committee every day until this one day, when I had to go and attend a meeting in my county, and then he sprung on this false evidence when I was not there to ask questions. The evidence he read was given when I was not present. I never like to strike below the belt. At that time the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did strike below the belt, he took advantage of me when I was not present, and I do not believe there is another man in the House or another minister who would have stooped to such a mean, low trick as he did.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is trying to attempt to trump up a charge against me of that kind, and take advantage of me in that -way, but so far as I am concerned I want to state here, so far as this little matter of mine is concerned, I never in my life went to any official or any member of the government and asked them to allow one man to be employed by me. In fact, the evidence shows that I said I would not allow any government official to have anything to do with my property. There is not an official there that will .swear that I ever asked him to put on any government officials for me. I never did, and I never had any account rendered to me because the statement was not true. I think this Sorel affair is one of the most outrageous things ever done in this country, and I think it is unfair for the Minister of Marine to put up this gentleman here a few minutes ago to try to iget out of this thing in this way. So far as I am concerned, I believe that this affair in connection with the member for Richelieu is one of the most disgraceful things that ever took place in the history of this country. I cannot believe for one minute that the right hon. the Prime Minister is satisfied with the way the Department of Marine is going on. The Minister of Marne has all his government officials at Prescott, and I have told him there is not Mr. SPEAKER.
*any doubt at all but that there has been the same kind of thievery going on there in the same -way right along.
Order.

But, if I wish to say what I think, I do not believe the minister cares whether it is going on or not as long as it benefits his party. That is the way I put it, because it is all his own political friends who seem to get these favours. And so it is all along the line. We have cases up there in the Public Accounts 'Committee that witnesses are keeping away because, as I believe, they don't want to expose 'the minister, so much graft is going on in that department. The Prime Minister surely must take cognizance of all those things going on there. If these statements are true in the press that he is going to appoint this man on the Supreme Court

Mr. REID (Grenville)-I think the Prime Minister is going pretty far if he does it. So far as the Minister of Marine is concerned there were other cases that really on account of the feeling we have towards him and others we did not investigate. Why, when he was appointed Minister of Marine the Prime Minister know-s well the statements that were going around this House about the position he occupied before that. Will the Prime Minister- look up and see that while he was Speaker of the House the amount he charged up to this government were such that no other Speaker of the House or any half dozen of them ever spent so much.

We have a head of the Marine and Fisheries Department, and we have a right to discuss these matters in connection with the man in charge of that department. I do not blame those fellows that are stealing from and robbing the Marine and Fisheries Department so long as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries either from ignorance or knowledge is willing to let it go on. It is -going on there, and it is either through his ignorance or within his knowledge, and any member of this House judging by his . past experience from what we have seen can judge which it is. So far as I am concerned," I have my own opinion and every other member can have his opinion. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty), men from -Quebec, men who

know the situation, don't hesitate to say that the public thieving and robbery that is going on at the Sorel works is publicly known all over the district of Montreal, an'd that being so surely the Prime Minister must know it. Is he going to allow this to go on? When I brought this matter up about the Marine Department a few years ago he stood up here and said he was going to clean out this department, going to purify it, and what is the record now? I tell him that if the previous minister, the late Hon. Raymond Prefontaine, could stand up here to-night and see the way this department is going on since he left it, he would be ashamed of the government for running it the way they have been doing since. The record of it is something awful. We can bring it before the Public Accounts Committee, but there is no notice taken of it. I tell the Prime Minister that if he is going to allow things to go on as they have been going on in that department his time will be limited.
We have heard that before.
I believe the Prime Minister thinks that the people will not stand for robbery. Will the Prime Minister say that the people will stand for robbery?

I rise to a point of order. I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but for the decorum of this House it is -time we should have your ruling Mr. Speaker, whether an hon. member of this House may be permitted to say that with the knowledge of a minister, whether the Prime Minister of the country or the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, thieving is going on, and thereby saying that the minister may be mentioned as a party to the crime, because-[DOT]
I cannot allow the hon. member to make a speech.
, flit down.

I ask your ruling, Mr. Speaker, on my point of order. I say that any member of this House who' charges a minister of the Crown with knowingly allowing thieving to go on in his department is making a statement that the minister himself is guilty of theft, and such a statement should not be allowed in the House.
I did not hear any such statement.

With regard to what the hon. member has stated about thieving and robbery going on at Sorel, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier made a statement in this House this afternoon,
on his responsibility as a member, that it was going on.
That does not prove that it is true.

It has been stated in this House that it is going on, and we have proved beyond a doubt that it has been going on. I made a statement in this House that it was going on, and the Prime Minister took me to task, and I proved it. He appointed Judge Cassels to inquire into it, and it was proved that it was going on. Why did the gentleman who made that statement not make some charge against me? No man ever made a charge against me, because they knew that it was not true; and another thing- they never sent me any account.
We are not built that way.

I do not wish to refer any more to this matter. I did not intend to make any statement on the affair, but it does seem to me pretty small that the Prime Minister, through his Minister of Marine and Fisheries, would put up a member to try to bolster up such an outrageous case of robbery and theft as this is, by citing my case. I do not think the Prime Minister would believe for one minute that I would be guilty of trying to do what these men say.
Oh, no.

I do not care what the gentlemen behind him say. I have that confidence in the Prime Minister, at any rate, that he would not think I would do anything of that kind. The hon. member has asked me something about the little question of gas. Well, to the best of my knowledge and belief, after questioning Mr. Fraser and the other gentlemen there, the value of the gas used-because I think it was used only one day-was about 50 cents. I explained at the time that the company I was connected with had given the government a right-of-way over our property for their railway, which they have got to-day, and I believe that Tight-of-way was worth anything from $1,000 -to $3,000, and they never charged them a cent. The company also gave the government the use of their wharf. The dredging they talk about, was, it is true, in front of a wharf owned by this company, tout it was done for the advantage of a wharf alongside owned by the government. I did not want it; I was not using that wharf; but the government boats were using it, and the dredging was in front of the company's wharf for the purpose of enabling the government boats to go to the wharf that was beside the wharf owned by the company

with which I was connected. It was done for their sole benefit. After that, down comes this private secretary, Mr. Wiallard, sent iby the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to see if he could not get up some cock-and-bull story for the purpose of injuring me. Well, I came before the electors, and the people there, including Liberals, were disgusted that any government would do so mean an act against any member. They could not believe it was true, and at the next -election, although the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as-I understood-because I heard on what I considered pretty good authority-sent some thousands of dollars in to try to defeat me
Order.
The hon. gentleman should not make that statement.

Well, I withdraw it, if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says it was not so. But notwithstanding that fact I had the largest majority I ever had, although more money was used against me than I believe was used at any other election, and I can judge from the rumours, of the source from which it game. I did believe that the evidence we had in the Publi-c Accounts Committee would have some effect on the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; I expected that we would have a better management of that department, but I must confess that knowing all the departments, even the Public Works Department, which the public think is so bad, in my judgment the Marine and Fisheries Department is the most disgracefully run department in the whole government. If there is robbery and thieving going on in the departments, that department is the worst of them all. Now, I do not intend saying any more. I simply rose because of the remarks made against me. I am not a bit afraid of what the minister or any member of the government or any member of this House can do against me in my constituency. I was born in that county, I have lived there all my life, I have run five elections there, and I am satisfied- that I can run another, even with the whole government against me, and I can have as big a majority -as I had at the last election.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I thought, Mr. Speaker, that we had met here to-night for the purpose of discussing the question which is now before the House-the report which has been made and which has been proposed by -the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), and the report which has been proposed, by the -hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I Mr. REID (Grenvillp)
find, however, by the speech which w-e have just heard, that we have gone absolutely out of the way and out of the rules which are generally followed in such cases. I want to say immediately to the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid), that when he says that I had something to do with the statement which has been made to-night in connection with the investigation which took place some years ago, or, to use the expression which he employed several times, that I had put up the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), he is making an assertion which is absolutely unfounded.
I had it several days ago that you were going to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I never spoke to the hon. member for Richmond in regard to it. I never mentioned the matter in any way, shape or form, to that hon. gentleman or to anybody else, and I am surprised at the statement of the hon. member for Grenville because he cannot show that anything of that kind came from me in any way whatever. When he makes that erroneous assertion I say that he does something which is absolutely unfair and uncalled for. However, I do not care very much, and I am glad that the hon. member has seen fit to speak of the administration' of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, because since I have had charge of the administration of that department I have tried to conduct its affairs in such a way as to enlist the confidence of the people.
You have not done it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I have done it not only to my own satisfaction but to the satisfaction of all fair-minded men in this country. 1 admit that at one time the department was under a cloud. What did I do? I took the necessary steps to investigate everything connected with the administration of the department. When the Civil Service Commission came into the department, I said to them that they could examine everything, and I put at their disposal all the papers which were in the department. Later on, when they stated that there were some frauds, or some general charges against the administration, or against some officials of the department, I asked my colleagues to appoint one of the most eminent judges in this country to investigate thoroughly the affairs of the department. If we had been afraid of any wrong-doing I never would have recommended such an investigation. But, I had the best lawyers in the country, I had one of the most eminent judges to be found in Canada, to investigate the affairs of the department, and when that investigation was over and when it was found that some

people were guilty of wrong-doing, I did not hesitate for one moment to recommend to my colleagues the dismissal of those officers who had violated the rules of honesty and rectitude. With regard to the statement that stealing and thievery are still going on, I may say to the hon. member for Grenville and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that I will always be disposed to do everything in my power to put an end to anything of that kind. The hon. member for Grenville says that there are steals going on still in Prescott. What would be the duty of the hon. member for Grenville in such a case as that? The hon. member for Jacques Cartier also stated this afternoon that in September or October last, he knew there was something irregular and illegal going on at Sorel. What would be the duty of these hon. gentlemen? Are they not obliged, like ministers of the Crown, to see that the administration is honestly carried on? If they know of something wrong in any branch of the public service is it not their duty as members of the House to advise the minister of the wrong-doing, or to get up in parliament and say what has been done? The hon. member for Jacques Cartier stated this afternoon that he was advised in September or October last that there was something wrong in Sorel. Why did he not come and tell me? Why did he not advise the minister what was going on? The hon. member for Grenville states also that there is some thieving going on in Prescott. If the hon. member knows that, it is his duty to get up and state what is going on and to give me the particulars in order that the guilty parties may be punished.
I will tell the minister why-because the minister, up in the Public Accounts Committee, defends these rascals instead of prosecuting them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The hon. member has the audacity to state that I am protecting rascality

Sure, you are.
Mr. BRODEUR

when I dismissed and
suspended no less than 29 officers of the service who had been found guilty by a Royal Commission I did this under my sense of duty and _ the next day the Montreal 'Gazette,' which is a respectable paper, praised the action which I then took. I say now that if there is thieving, if there is stealing in some parts of the department, it is the duty of any member to see that these steals are put a stop to and to denounce these things. My hon. friend can bring his facts before the Public Accounts Committee, he can state the facts to. the minister and he will always find that I will take the necessary steps to prevent any stealing or wrong-doing. I may say in connection with this matter
that some time ago a member of the opposition, anxious, I am sure, that the administration should be honestly carried out, bi ought to my notice something which was wrong and I immediately advised the necessary inquiry with the view of punishing the guilty parties. I may inform my hon. friend that in spite of everything that he has said to-night against me, I will always receive any information which he will give in that respect and he may be sure that the necessary steps will be taken to put an end to any wrong-doing which may be disclosed. The hon. member for Grenville has thought fit to refer to all sorts of things with which I have been connected. I say that I am not afraid to put my record before parliament and before the country. My record is just as good as that of any member of this House. I have been trying to do my duty and I think I have done it. I have punished and dismissed culprits, I have sent to jail persons against whom I have been able to secure convictions and I will punish wrong-doing so long as I have anything to do with the administration of the public affairs of this country.
I do not want to discuss at any great length the question which is now engaging the attention of the House. But, perhaps I may be permitted to say a word or two as to the circumstances which surrounded that question. In the month of May last, the hon. memeber for Richelieu seeing that he could not get workmen in Sorel to paint his house went to the time-keeper of the shipyard to ask if he could procure the services of some men for this purpose. There is no great harm in that.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Certainly not. What harm could there be so long as there is no fraud, and the public service does not suffer? Some hon. members opposite say this cannot be. I say, on the contrary, that sometimes it is even a good thing to do in order to retain the services of men who are employed in the government works there. The men employed in the government works in Sorel are generally very good men, and fulfil their duties in a very satisfactory manner. But there may be times in the year when there is not so much to do, and, if we have a chance to secure work for our men elsewhere, it means that we shall be able to retain their services. I do not see how it can be stated that the mere fact that the member for Richelieu asking for men to work on his house is a very bad thing. Some time ago we had a case where we did not absolutely need the services of a certain man, but had we dismissed him he would have gone 1 elsewhere and we would have lost the I services of a man we could not easily

replace. We found some work for him outside the yard, and I say in such a case there is no harm in it, on the contrary, it is 'to the advantage of the yard.
Did the minister continue to pay that man?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
No. But when I made my first proposition I had in mind the suggestion of some hon. members opposite that this should not be done in any case. I say that sometimes it should be done. The circumstances under which the hon. member for Richelieu made his request for men were these:	His wife was, unfortunately, very ill. He was unable to stay in Sorel, but had to remain with her at Saranac Lake, where she was being treated. He asked the foreman whether he could not get some men, and the foreman, Mr. Champagne, answered that he could get these men. In June a few days' work was done. Mr. Lanctot was absent most of the time. A few days' more work was done in July, but properly speaking, the painting was done in September and October, and finished in November. So far, there is certainly no harm. Mr. Lanctot asked the foreman painter Mr. Page where he could get the paints for his house. It was suggested that he could get them from Cyrille Labelle & Co., but on that remark the foreman said that he did not know -whether it would be possible to get all the paint from that firm, that there might be 'some qualities that they would not have. Mr. Lanctot said that in such a case Mr. Page could supply the paints and he would see that they were replaced. Mr. Page agreed. That is all that was done. As to the men there was no agreement except -that they were to be paid by Mr. Lanctot. Nobody suggested the contrary; nobody suggests that Mr. Lanctot was not to pay these men. The best evidence is that during the progress of the work Mr. Lanctot asked several times for his bill. What was done in this case by Mr. Champagne? Mr. Champagne did what I consider a very irregular thing, but under circumstances which I think it only fair the House should understand. Mr. Champagne had known other instances of men being set at work outside, and he had paid these men, having the money from the person for whom they were working. But Mr. Champagne was severely criticised, so he tells us, and some of .the men insinuated that he had put some of the money in his pocket which otherwise would have gone to them. To protect himself, without the knowledge of Mr. Lanctot and without the knowledge of the officers of the department, he kept .these men on the pay-lists, but without any intention of defrauding anybody. He had no intention of stealing the money or doing anything wrong; he acted Mr. BRODEUR.
as he did simply for the purpose of protecting himself against such insinuations as has been made against him. And when the work was finished his statement of account was sent to Mr. ^Lanctot, and immediately a cheque vras returned for an amount, and the transaction was consequently closed.
Now, with regard to the paint, it was understood that the paint should be taken from Mr. Cyrill Labelle, but at the same time it was agreed between Mr. Page and Mr. Lanctot that if the latter could not get all the paint he required for his house, he might get it from the department. Mr. Page was the foreman of the painters. We put at his disposal from the stores a certain quantity of paint which is not charged to any particular work, because this paint has to be mixed, and when it is mixed it is used on different works. Mr. Page renders every week	an account to	the shipyard
cost clerk stating the amount he has spent upon such and such a work. In that way he has at his disposal a certain quantity of paint, and out of that he took a small quantity to be used on Mr. Lanctot's house. It was understood that the paint was to be returned, it has been returned, or has been paid for. So far as the money is concerned, it cannot be said that there was any theft, or anj conspiracy amounting to a crime. The hon. member for Ste. Anne (Mr. Doherty) has tried to show that there was theft under the circumstances, and that word is also to be found in the charges made by the member for Champlain. But I am convinced, and I am sure the majority of the members of this House are convinced, that there was no theft in the circumstances which have been proven. What constitutes theft? There must be an intention to steal, to defraud. Was there any intention shown to defraud in these circumstances? Certainly not. Was there any intention of stealing? Certainly not; it cannot possibly be said that any crime has been proven. What is the situation today? A minority report has been brought down signed by the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker). Do these two hon. gentlemen in their report intimate that there was a crime, that there was robbery? Not at all, they simply state that it was a violation of the Independence of Parliament.
We said it was unlawful.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
But they do not say it was a criminal offence, they do not say that there was theft, they do not say that the charges made by the member for Champlain have been proved. The member for Champlain charges that there was a theft committed. The hon. member for Hamilton does not say that, and I would be greatly

surprised if he should now say that there was theft under the circumstances. How does it come then that these charges of theft are now being made? The Minister of Justice showed conclusively that there was no violation of the Independence of Parliament Act, and after his speech the member for Ste. Anne's discovered that the motion made by the member for Jacques Cartier could not stand criticism. Then hon. gentlemen opposite started these charges of theft and robbery. Well, I say there is absolutely nothing in the evidence whicli would justify the charge on the part either of the foreman or of Mr. Lanctot. Why is Mr. Lanctot being prosecuted to-day? Why have these charges been, made against him? Of course, we should not refuse to receive information, no matter from what source it comes. Who brought these charges against Mr. Lanctot? Who are the men who have been surrounding the member for Champlain and urging him on to make these charges against the member for 'Richelieu? It is well known that if Mr. Lanfitot had been willing to get the Department of Marine and Fisheries to make a certain contract with a certain gentleman whose letters are filed in this case, if Mr. Lanctot had been willing to support the contentions of the man who wanted to blackmail the department, who wanted to get a contract with the department that we were not willing to make, there would have been no charges against Mr. Lanctot. Hon. members of this House who have followed the investigation know that a certain gentleman was applying for a contract with the department, he wanted to sell us some machinery that we did not need, and I informed the hon. member for Richelieu that we were not going to purchase that machinery. This man's name was Lamoureux, and Mr. Lanctot informed him that the department was not going to purchase his goods, that they were of no use to us.
At what date?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Some time in the month of September and October, also in November. Then, what does Mr. Lamoureux do? He writes a letter to Mr. Lanctot on the 23rd of November, 1910, page 185, of the evidence. This is what he says:
My Dear Adelard,-What news will you bring me Saturday? You will have seen the minister, I suppose. I count on your bringing me a favourable reply.
If the minister refuses to grant me what I ask of him, after 'having made promises to me, and having heard what he has said to me, if he refuses, I say, I declare to you, my dear Lanctot, that I will be obliged to attack strongly and to bring to light things about Which I feel reluctant. My determination has reached its height, whatever may be the consequence.
Do your best, my dear Lanctot, because a refusal will certainly have grave consequences.
You have enough in hand to make the minister give in, if he keeps his word, and what he has written, as I have no doubt he will.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) J. O. LAMOUREUX.
Here is a letter which speaks fox itself. He states in his letter that I made him some promise to purchase his machinery. I saw the man some time afterwards and said:	On what do you rely in stating I
have given you a promise? You know I have been refusing all the time to purchase these goods, because we do not need them. He said: It is true, but I have done it in order to induce Lanctot to do still more towards you and to induce him to work more strongly in my favour and to represent me. He felt it was only just to write me the following letter:
If from the letter which I addressed to Mr. Lanctot, our member, on the 23rd November, 1910, the inference was drawn that I was making malevolent insinuations against you, I state that my thoughts were not translated properly.
I had not the slighest intention in the world of attacking or tarnishing your reputation. On the contrary, I have never ceased to regard your reputation and your character as absolutely unattackable, and. in addition to that, Mr. Minister, I have no reason to doubt your perfect honesty.
Perhaps my letter was not sufficiently precise for those whose interest it is to alienate from me your esteem. However, it appears to me evident, in its entirety, that the hard words it contains are for him to whom it was addressed, and not for you, Mr. Minister, because I have always thought that if I did not obtain that which I asked, it was because Mr. Lanctot did not take the interest in me that I had hoped from him. Several times he showed himself very reticent.
If in my letter I speak of promises and of encouragements that you could have given me, it was the object of stimulating the zeal of Mr. Lanctot and of proving to him you were not as strongly opposed to my requests as he wished to make me believe.
Once more, Mr. Minister, I have never for an instant doubted your perfect honesty, and I have never wished to tarnish your reputation.
These explanations would have been unnecessary, I am convinced, Mr. Minister, had not the persons interested in depriving me of your esteem sought to draw from any letter a meaning which I had no intention of conveying.
I am confident, Mr. Minister, that my explanations will satisfy you and that you will continue to believe in my best consideration and most respectful sentiments.
Your humble servant,
(Sgd.) J. O. LAMOUREUX.
A regular patent medicine letter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
That is a very significant letter. Here is a man who some time ago stated that if a certain contract which he was expected to make was not consum-

mated, he would make some revelations and he said the minister had given him a promise. Then he writes a letter stating that he did that just to induce Mr. Lanctot to work more strongly for him. That explains to a very large extent the charges which were later made in this House. I do not know if the member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin) is here or not, but if he is here I suppose he will admit that this man Lamoureux has been one of those who have approached him and induced him to make these charges against Mr. Lanctot. Who are the other men who had instigated chiefly these charges against Mr. Lanctot. Two men were in the service in Sorel whose services we had been obliged to dispense with. These men come later on and say: We worked at Mr. Lanctot's house for a couple of months. One of them said he had been working there for four months and that he was being paid by the government during all that time. Honest man! Did he come and tell his superior officers that he was at the same time working for the government and also for Mr. Lanctot. That he was stealing from the government? Why did he not go and say to the director of the shipyard: We are in receipt of money from the government which we do not earn. No, but afterwards, when they were dismissed and sent away from the work of the department those men went to see my hon. friend from Champlain (Mr. Blondin) in connection with the men who wanted to blackmail Mr. Lanctot and they started these charges which are now made against Mr. Lanctot.

Does the hon. minister not know that every material fact spoken
of by these witnesses has been admitted by Pagd and Champagne?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
It has been stated several times here by members who have spoken on the other side that the member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin) should not be blamed for anything in connection with the charges which have been made before this House. I say the hon. member should have stated when he made his charges that the amount had been paid by Mr. Lanctot. It was a very important fact, why did he not state it? He simply took the statements of these men Lamoureux, who wanted to blackmail Mr. Lanctot, Douaire and Proulx, who had been dismissed from the service of the department. Of course every member is free to take evidence from any person, I admit that, but at the same time I think the word of those men who had been dismissed from the public service for cause should not be received and accepted so readily and more especially that charges of thi9 serious nature should not be brought against fellow-members of this Mr. BRODEUR.
House upon such testimony. I am sure the members of this House should be convinced now that the charges made against Mr. Lanctot were not well founded, that he did not violate the Independence of Parliament Act, and that he did not commit any theft or crime as suggested by the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) and the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers). Under these circumstances I say that we should clear the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Lanctot) of the charges which have been made against him.
As the House is aware, the hon member for Richelieu (Mr. Lanctot) was placed in a very trying position. He was obliged to be absent from his city a great deal in order to be with and to nurse his wife, who was very ill. In that situation, he had the sympathy of every man in Sorel, every man was willing to help him; and because some men may have been a little indiscreet in the way they extended sympathy to him, I say that we should not, under the circumstances, do anything which would add to his anxiety.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I will refer in the first place to the words that the hon. the Minister of Marine has just uttered. He tells us that he asks nothing better than to be duly informed of what is taking place. For my part I shall not fail to tell him of the abuses and thefts committed, especially at the Sorel works. I hold here a certain number of affidavits concerning those frauds, and there are many others. The abuses referred to have taken place within a year at the Sorel yards, and the minister should know of therm

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: (Translation.) The hon. member is doubtless aware that six accused persons have been arrested.

(Translation.) But have you held an investigation such as will satisfy public opinion? I may tell you that had such an investigation been held the hon, member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin) would never have pressed his charges.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: (Translation.) An investigation was held two years ago.
(Translation.) It was not a complete investigation. In any case I *could, if Inacessjary, produce some fifty affidavits concerning the abuses taking place at Sorel; if I may be allowed to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: (Translation.) If the hon. member will hand me the affidavits in his possesssion, I will hold an investigation immediately.

(Translation.) We on this side of the House do- not want Mr. Lanctot's

head; we require an investigation satisfactory to the public and which will throw light upon the doings of certain government employees at Sorel. I might mention certain names, in fact I will do in the course of my remarks. A certain Mr. Oscar Champagne-for there are several of the name-who checks and prepares pay lists, is said to have answered; ' I do not want to have anything to do with the payment of the men, as I would be accused of not giving them their full pay.' That the government would pay them and Mr. Lanctot refund the money. Men's services have been loaned and honestly so to certain persons in Sorel. There is nothing to be said against that. There is, for instance, the case of Amable Lussier, who secured the services of government painters; he paid them himself and they did not report on such days as having worked for the government. Might not Mr. Champagne have said to Mr. Lanctot; If you want painters you will get them, but you must pay them yourself. An appeal to sentiment is made on the ground that Mr. Lanctot's wife was v'ery ill when the work began. I fail to see why this is constantly brought before the public. A man of courage would not resort to such means for the purpose of attracting sympathy and condoning actions of which the public cannot .approve. Concerning the illness of Mrs. Lanctot, I sympathize with the member for Richelieu, but I do not approve of the tactics which consist in calling attention to the illness of the lady in order to attract sympathy to himself. Mr. Lanctot's wife should not be called in to protect him.
At all events, was the hon. gentleman constantly at Saranac lake? Was he not at Sorel on June 3 when the work began? He spent most of his time at Sorel. There was no such pressing haste as has been contended and he might easily have seen Mr. Papineau and made arrangements with him to obtain more men. It is established that Mr. Papineau was only two days absent, May 28 and 29. It will not be believed that the member for Richelieu might not have met him had he so wished.
The organization of the Sorel shipyards should be known. We should be in a position to decide whether it is imperfect or incomplete. There are legions of employees there.
The investigation which has just taken place has given us and the public much information. If, as I have just remarked, the organization is not perfect, it is at least complete in this sense that there are numerous employees of all classes and kinds. It is not perfect because it has been found wanting in a verv simple matter.
Papineau is the manager of the Sorel shipyards. His assistant is Mr. H. A. Terreault.
(Translation.) Will the hon. member allow me to ask whether the member for Richelieu made any effort to^see the deputy manager of the Sorel works on finding that the manager was absent?

(Translation.) Not the slightest. On May 28 or 29 he called at the office of Mr. Papineau who happened to be absent at Montreal. He made no effort to see Mr. Terreault, nor did he seek to meet Mr. Papineau on his return.
Mr. Alfred Baril is the accountant. Mr. Norman Masse is keeper of the stores in which the materials employed in construction work at Sorel are kept.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: (Translation.) Does the hon. member know anything against Mr. Baril?

I will hand in affidavits against Mr. Baril and if I am not mistaken I can get several.
Mr. Jean Baptiste Page is foreman of painters. Mr. Arthur Lavallee, his assistant, distributes the paint for different works. Mr. Cecil Doutre is the purchasing agent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Mr. Doutre does not reside at Sorel.

Whether he resides at Montreal or at Sorel he is supposed to form part of the staff. Mr. Oscar Champagne is time-keeper; he also prepares the pay lists. The branch dealing with the cost of construction is under the direction of Mr. Ulric Latraverse, with Mr. Albert Prud-homme as assistant. Both have books to keep; by means of statements furnished by other branches, they aTe in a position to compute the cost of all construction or other works in the Sorel shipyards. Mr. Desire Champagne is paymaster. Mr. Cuthbert Champagne is keeper of the 'punch' by means of which the men register their time. Mr. Napoleon Badeau is foreman of the wood construction. Mr. Gendron is foreman of day labourers.
There are a number of other employees whose names I will not mention. Each man working at the Sorel shipyard is given a number and every different work is also numbered. The organization cost $42,000 and it is now found defective. It was devised by one Falconer and supposed to be excellent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Does the hon. member contend that such a sum was spent for that organization or that Mr. Falconer appointed those employees?

It cost $42,315.02 to establish a good system of book-keeping and instruct the assistants.
We find therefore at Sorel an army of employees, managers, assistants, guardians,

time-keepers, foremen who rub up and seemingly interfere with one another. All are bound to protect the property of the government and of the people at Sorel. However, in spite of this complicated machinery there -was found to be, in the year of grace 1910, a man, a lawyer by profession, who succeeded in having his house painted and by government materials, tools and men and at the cost of the government. The work was begun as soon as the house was ready to be painted, i.e. the 3rd June, 1910, and was finished only on the 21st November following.
During that period of about 23 weeks, government men and government paint *were used for that private work. Until the 21st November seven or eight men at a time worked there and were paid regularly by the government every two weeks. An extraordinary feature is that the government was officially informed of this only on the 22nd November, 1910, by a statement of the wages of painters and labourers accompanied by a cheque for $375.62, addressed to Mr. L. G. Papineau, the manager. The statement was handed in by Jean Baptiste Page, who -was not the official book-keeper but assumed those duties for the occasion.
Mr. Papineau must have been very much surprised on receiving such a statement and cheque! Until then the government was kept in the most absolute ignorance concerning the painting of this now notorious house. The cheque covered the payment of wages only and not the cost of material. The matter now being known, steps were taken to recover the cost of paint and other material, and Mr. Papineau determined the mode in which this recovery should be made. He decided to obtain the paints from a Montreal firm-the Mount Royal Colour & Varnish Company-to the amount of $81.60 and to return it in kind to the government. Mr. Papineau gave his personal cheque in payment. The goods reached Sorel on December the 12th, 1910 and were stored by the department on the 13th.
The hon. member for Richelieu repaid Mr. Papineau the amount of his personal cheque and also the cost of transportation. But how was the whole of this 'tour de force' managed? for in reality it is a 'tour de force.' Very simple and the matter as a whole shows the true value of the army of government employees at Sorel.
The hon. member for Richelieu spoke first of all to Mr. Oscar Champagne, the timekeeper, whose office is next to that of the manager, Mr. Papineau and of Mr. Terreault, the assistant manager. He said to him:-Mr. Papineau is not in his office, can you send me painters as my house is ready to be painted? With pleasure, re-Mr. NANTEL
plied Mr. Champagne. The member for Richelieu met Mr. Jean Baptiste Page, foreman painter, as he left Mr. Champagne's office, and repeated the same request; can you send me any painters? With pleasure replied Mr. Page, if Mr. Papineau consents.
Some time later, between the 15tli and the 20th May, according to some *witnesses, between the 15th and the 30th, according to others, but in any ease before the month of June, as the painting began on June 3, the member for Richelieu had asked Page for paint and material, requesting him to keep a seperate account, as all would be returned. It was not more difficult than that. That is all. Nothing was done towards seeing Mr. Papineau, although he was absent from Sorel only on the 28th and 29th May, two days in all. It was not worth while to see him or his assistant. Neither Jean Baptiste Page nor Oscar Champagne cared to see Mr. Papineau and submit the case to him.
Thus, from the 3rd June to the 21st November, government paint,, material, brushes, were abundant, painters, and even labourers flocked the house in question.
It has been attempted, in the course of the investigation, to prove that it was not possible to find painters at Sorel; but laborers at least could be obtained.
At all events, from June 3rd, all the government employees were placed at the disposal of Mr. Lanctot without anything being changed or disturbed in the routine of the yards. Painters and labourers registered each day as if working for the government, when they could; when they could not do so themselves, Cuthbert Champagne, the complainant guardian of the 'punch' registered' for them, having been so instructed by his namesake Oscar Champagne. Then Oscar Champagne, who alone with his pal Jean Baptiste Page knew what was going on, prepared his pay list regularly and, each fortnight, and painters doing the private work of the member for Richelieu, were paid by the government,
As I have said, each work bears a special number and all the employees engaged upon it are also numbered, so that it is quite possible, if the rule be observed, to compute the cost of each undertaking. The director of construction work can give, at any time, a statement of the cost of any one undertaking. In the present case that was not done. For the work in question was carried on outside of the knowledge of the manager, Mr. Papineau; it was kept secret from him and done behind his back, although his office was next to that of Oscar Champagne and the house in question a few yards away from his own residence; the whole according to a secret and collusive understanding between the hon. member for Richelieu, Oscar Champagne and Jean Baptiste Page, under the higher direction of Mr. Baril.

Nothing of this private work, conducted by two subordinate employees of the government, appeared in the regular books of the department at Sorel. J. B. Page, foreman, appears to have noted the men's work in his personal note book or on loose sheets which he handed to Oscar Champagne. The latter kept them in a private drawer and manufactured or falsified the pay lists every two months, making it appear that the men had really worked for the government. In this manner was prepared the account of $375.60 handed to L. G. Papineau on November 22nd, 1910, with a cheque for $375.60 bearing the same date, which was charged and deposited in the Federal Treasury on January 11th, 1911
Is my hon. friend now reading from the evidence?
Is that what you are anxious about?
Yes, because you have no right to read your speech.

It is an extract from the evidence. In any case, I am in the hands of the Speaker.
At the Sorel shipyards, in order to obtain material from the stores, paint, for instance, a written requisition is required. It appears that in spite of this rule, the foreman may obtain large quantities of paint and in fact it is from what friend Jean Baptiste Page had in hand and which he had obtained for other purposes and other works, that he furnished the member for Richelieu with the material for painting his house.
J. B. Page appears to have noted on a blotter the amount of paint and material so furnished, the value of which amounted to $81.60. But, most unfortunately, the blotter was lost as soon as the account had been prepared and it has been impossible to find it. Had it been lost beforehand, what would have been the position of the member for Richelieu? It is evident that this matter of paint was not an ordinary one and that it required all the influence that a government member of parliament may exercise over government officials at the Sorel shipyards to persuade them to take the chances they did.
It will also be admitted that in computing the cost of this undertaking, the bookkeeping we have had before us is very crude and rudimentary when we reflect upon the fine organization obtaining at Sorel. Quite plainly Messrs. J. B. Page and Oscar Champagne are by no means official but rather under the circumstances officious accountants.
If they were acting in good faith and anxious to do everything openlv and above board as is their boast, why did they not proceed in the usual manner prescribed for every undertaking in the Sorel shipyards? If it was desired to paint the house of the
member for Richelieu, why *was not a special number given to the undertaking? So much paint might then have been requisitioned for and charged against the number assigned to the work. All the statements would then have been transmitted to Mr. Ulrie Latraverse, who, immediately after the completion of the work, would have stated: the cost is so much, neither more nor less. The matter would have been clear, clean and no more said.
But it is contended that this was a loan of men and of material. During the investigation, Mr. Amable Lussier told us that on a certain occasion, the department had loaned painters to repair his premises. But he paid those men himself; there was no connivance between the men and their foreman to register as if working for the government. He also paid for the material.
Mr. Napoleon Badeau, superintedent of wood construction and foreman of carpenters, also loaned men to Mr. Lanotot, but he made sure that they did not register as if working for the government.
Speaking of Mr. Badeau, do you know, Mr. Speaker, that if Mr. Badeau had not been superintending the wood construction at the Sorel shipyards, if in his place there had been a man less anxious to do his duty, less scrupulous, a man in fact of the stamp of Page and Champagne, instead of having to pay the cost of the paint only at the house in question, the carpentering and woodwork would have come in as well. If you doubt it, listen to Mr. Badeau's deposition at the investigation ; it is the evidence of an honest man. And really, had a minister of the Crown not testified therein. I would say that Mr. Napoleon Badeau is the most honest man -heard before the committee.
Here is an extract which I find at page 179 of the printed evidence:	,

what he wanted. I told him I had it not at the time, hut that it could easily he prepared. I told him then, that to hare what he wanted, he would have to ask Mr. Papineau first.
