(Translation). Since this discussion has been opened, we are witnessing, Mr. Speaker, a somewhat strange spectacle. I understand how the hon. member for Terrebonne has been able to draw certain conclusions from the evidence submitted, but what I cannot make out is about the hon. members on the left who have preceded him, because they do not agree with him. Before proceeding any further, I will beg leave to read the conclusions of the minority, so as to see if the hon. gentlemen will concur in what the hon. member for Terrebonne has just said.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who has signed the report jointly with the member for Hamilton East, has said:
' We conclude, moreover, that the said Ade-lard Lanctot, by the acts and proceedings as aforesaid, has violated the independence of parliament.'
What can the hon. members who have signed that report say as against the declarations of the hon. member for Terrebonne? He has just said that the independence of parliament has not been violated. Still, those hon. members have read the same evidence and they are in presence of the same proceedings.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to draw your attention on the accusations brought against the member for Richelieu. The thing is very serio-us, and when the hon. member for Terrebonne says that he has nothing against him, I must confess I do not know what he means. But it is he who is accused; it is he whom they are seeking to ruin; it is he who is accused of being a thief, a highway thief, who is accused of robbery. [DOT]
Does my hon. friend for Champlain know what is meant by such a word? If he knows the meaning of it, he has been somewhat rash in his accusations. Because his hon. friends who have discoursed this afternoon and to-night have objected to reach those conclusions, they say that it. is due to a mistake if the English text contains that- word.
Has mv hon. friend ever Tead the Cr'm-Mr. NANTEL
inal Code before using such a word? Let me draw his attention on section 445 which defines the word 'Robbery':
Robbery is theft accompanied with violence or threats of violence to any person or property used to extort the property stolen, or to prevent or overcome resistence to its being stolen.
If the hon. member for Champlain had read those articles of the Criminal Code he would not have dared to make such a charge. As he did not know the meanmg of it, I will readily forgive him. He has never studied the laws of his country. He is more versed in the ' pills of his jiro-fession.
He is a notary.
I have never practiced medicine. I ask my hon. friend to withdraw that word. I am a notary, not a doctor.

Well, I will change the formula. If you are a notary, you are the more guilty, because notaries are acquainted with the law, perhaps not the criminal law; but in any case, your colleagues are ashamed and reject that accusation. Your colleagues have just told you that you were not right' in accusing the member for Richelieu of robbery.
Whom do you mean?

The learned member for Terrebonne has just said who it was. Before signing a mandate of that kind one must be careful. When a plaintiff goes before a court of justice in a case of robbery, the judge does not proceed before having had a preliminary inquest. In the present case such a charge cannot foe substantiated, and not a single member of the left has even attempted to do it.
We have heard of theft, of breach of trust, of malversation. I have listened attentively to all that has been said. I have studied the evidence, I have read and reread it and I say that not a single reasonable man acquainted with the criminal law would pretend that the evidence is sufficient to lay ground for an accusation of robbery. I challenge anybody to prove that the evidence on file would be accepted by a magistrate. The hon. member for Richelieu may have been perhaps imprudent, but I repeat that nothing has been proven to substantiate an accusation of robbery. All that is only a false pretense and we all know what i'3 meant by that.
Let them read the law, to know what is meant by false pretenses. Evidently, those hon. gentlemen who had a grudge against the department now attack the member for Richelieu and make him pay for the bad temper that they feel. We have the admission of one of your own men. My hon.

friend of Terrebonne has just declared that there is no grudge against my hon. friend of Richelieu, but rather against the Marine Department. Then, why don't you behave like brave and courageous men, and don't you lay a direct accusation against the hon. Minister of Marine, with your own seats at stake.
If it is true that this department is as corrupted as you say, and that infamous things are there going on, you-ought to have enough courage to make a formal accusation against the hon. minister whom you are seeking to ruin in public opinion by insinuations rather than direct accusations, because you know very well that you would not be able to prove them. In your ill-temper, you throw yourselves on the back of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier ... I beg pardon to my learned friend, it is he himself who goes for the hon. member for Richelieu.
The hon. member for Champlain ought to have known that my hon. friend of Richelieu had pledged himself to reimburse the government, and that therefore there could not have been neither a theft nor an intention of theft. I understand that his declaration has been made too late, but it was nevertheless too daring. If you examine the evidence, you can see that the declaration of reimbursement has been made at the very origin of this transaction, before anything had yet been delivered. I say that in such a case, it is impossible to prove an accusation of theft. Nobody who has studied criminal law would dare sustain such'a pretension. There must be, for a crime, an intention of criminality. Now, in this circumstance, there has never been any intention of theft. I prefer the declaration of the member for Terrebonne who tells us that the intention was primarily to have a general inquiry into what is going on in the Marine Department at Sorel. But then, why now call the member for Richelieu a thief, a highway robber? After the spectacle that they have given us, I am sur I should have good reason to doubt their sincerity.
They say that because Mr. Page and Champagne have proceeded irregularly, it follows that the member for Richelieu is a thief. Even if Page and Champagne had acted as the member for Jacques Cartier has said they have ; even if they had had no right to act as they have done; even if they had acted with imprudence and without authorization, should the conclusion be that there has been a theft? But every day our courts are asked to waive illegal contracts, things that there was no right to do. 'Should we perforce come to the conclusion that those persons are thiefs? It is an 'easy thing to say, but the proof of it is another affair.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier says that the evidence of Page is not to be believed. That is what he says, but where is the proof of it? Who was it that doubted the sincerity of that witness? Where can you see in the inquiry that the declaration under oath of that witness has been contested? One should never forget the principle that the evidence of a witness holds good, so long as the regularity or the sincerity of a witness has not been contested. Where can you see in the evidence that his sincerity has ever been questioned ? You are proceeding against this witness * ex iparte.' But why not give him the chance that is not refused to the greatest criminal to pay his debt. That is agreed, on the floor of the House everything is allowed when it comes to proffer an accusation; hut outside of this House, you would not dare to make a charge of perjury against this very same man.
They say that the work was done a.t Mr. Lanctot's house, next door to where lives the inspector-in-chief Mr. Papineau, and that no permission had been obtained from this gentleman. Would that constitute a theft? Even if Mr. Papineau had not been consulted; even if it had been shown that Champagne and Page had gone beyond their powers, and that they had no mandate to act as they have done, would that constitute a theft? If all those who overstep their-powers had to go to jail, I know some people who would not be here. If, for instance, the member for Champlain admits that he has exceeded his mandate; if he was asked to just'fy this accusation; if he was told: you have been imprudent, reckless, you have acted wickedly in proffering such art accusation against the member for Richelieu, what would he answer to that?
I hear some of those hon. gentlemen laughing. You can laugh, hut the wife and the children of the member for Richelieu are not in the same agreeable mood.
I make a call to order. If we want to uphold the dignity of the deliberations of this House, I must ask the hon.. member for Montcalm to please address; himself to the Speaker and not to members.

I have just said to the hon. member the accuser that he could have a laugh over what he had done, but ! that the one he has accused is not in the I same mood, since this wicked accusation has been made against him. He will never j be able to repair the wrong he has done to 1 that family. I have no doubt whatever that the member for Richelieu will be exonerated; but the result of that wicked accusation which has been hawked about' every where, and which stand in bold letters, in the press of the country, as a splendid advertisement for the member for Champlain, the result, I say, will he an incalculable wrong for the member for Richelieu, a wrong which the member for Champlain will never be able to repair for himself and his family.

They say that the work had been going on next door to Mr. Papineau. Well, the member for Richelieu who had asked Champagne and Page to do that work had a right to believe, from the answer received from those two men, that they had permission to do the work. Nothing could be more natural and .more logical. When those men came to do that work, it was because they had had the permission of Mr. Papineau. _
When an officer or a civil servant is asked to do a thing, if he answers : Very well, but I will ask permission of my chief. And if on the morrow I see that man at work, my conclusion is that the necessary permission has been granted.
They say that Mr. Papineau is an honest man. Others are in doubt or unwilling to say so. Who is to be believed ? The necessary conclusion is that Mr. Papineau knew what was going on, and that the member for Richelieu was in no necessity, as was said, to make further inquiries about it, since the men he had asked for were at work.
Will the hon. member allow me to ask him a question ? Has he read that part of the evidence of Mr. Papineau, in which he declares that he has no knowledge of what was going on ?

We hear, as an accepted fact, of the frightful things that are going on at Sorel. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has not been very affirmative on that point, but the member for Terrebonne went farther than that. He told us that abuses and frauds were going on there. But we are not obliged to believe all that. It is easy to throw accusations to the wind. When I am studying a case, I read the evidence and the affirmations made ' ex parte ' have to be controlled.
I may be allowed, I think, not to entertain the same opinion. The people in Sorel are just as respectable as anywhere else. They are honest and industrious. You say that there are scandals going on, but you show no proof of that.
At the time that those hon. gentlemen were in power, the finances of the country were in a sore plight. But now that we have a liberal government, millions of dollars keep flowing to us and this yeaT we have a surplus of thirty millions. You have never been able to show as much. Those hon. gentlemen are still going through the same dreams and they think they are still in power. They should not forget, however, that we are in power since 1896, and that is why the millions keep coming to us.
The member for Jacques Cartier has said: There has been nothing entered in the books. That is a gratuitous affirmation and one which must be taken subject to verification The evidence shows the contrarv. Books have been kept, and statements'regularly Mr. LAFORTUNE.
made every night. Why not state the true facts ? It is true there was no ledger ; there was perhaps no ledger. But for that kind of work, there is no necessity of books in double entry for the time of the men and the few materials which were brought there.
That is then a gratuitous affirmation, and we are not obliged to accept his 'ipse dixit'. I would rather rely on the evidence.
My learned friend has said it is a trick. We are playing no tricks, in our party, that is something to new for us. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier may know a good deal about tricks. Well, let him keep the patent of it, if he has it.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who is a professor at Laval, must be acquainted with that part of the law where it is admitted that the sending of materials, to the knowledge of those who possess them, does not constitute a theft and does not justify a writ of imprisonment. You can come to the law firm to which I have the honour to belong since five years, and you will be told that such an accusation cannot be deemed sufficient to get your man arrested. There may have been an imprudence, but when it comes to a question of having a man arrested, to ruin that man and to deprive him of what is most dear to him in the world, one must look at it twice before leaping.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has just declared, in contradiction to what the member for Elgin has said a moment ago, that there was no conspiration. The member for Elgin says :	They are conspirators.
Who is to be believed ? When, in doubt, there should be no condemnation.
When I see that the accusers themselves do not agree, I cannot help having serious doubts. One says white the other says black. If there has been conspiration, then I ask where is the fraud? I have no need to remind you that fraud must not be presumed. Who has proven it? Where is the witness? Is it not the accused who has to prove his innocence; but it belongs to the accuser to show where lies the culpability of the one he accuses. The proof then lies with you. If you cannot show that nroof, then the accused is acquitted. What you say is not sufficient to prove that d't is the truth. Where is the witness who has shown that theTe had been a theft or an intention of fraud, or even the existence of a false pretense? On the contrary, the intention to reimburse has been expressed at the very origin.
That the accused may have been imprudent, I concur with you in that. I belong to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. I have been present at all the meetings of this committee. I have listened to what has been said in this House. I have read all the evidence', and I say

that is simply a case of imprudence that that does not transgress the (independence which a member must possess. But to allege that my hon. friend for Richelieu must perforce be a thief, that he has committed' highway robbery, that he has taken possession of things under false pretenses, you will read that in the 'Devoir', but it is not true. It is a doctrine which has no currency. It may be heard in partisan papers, in speeches of small importance, but it is evident that my hon. friend for Richelieu has incurred neither censure nor blame, as those hon. iriembers of the left would fain have us believe.
Can it be said that the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who has signed the minority report, is this time in the right? I do not mean that he is not habitually in the right. A man cannot be acquitted nor forgiven because of his intention to reimburse. There are a great many criminals in our penitentiaries who would gladly reimburse, if they could be liberated on that chance. But in these cases, it is paying after the accusation has been proved, and after sentence has been pronounced. Even if a convict would be ready to pay, that would be too late. He could thus satisfy his conscience, but for human law it would be too late.
I have some experience of it, Mr. Speaker. Every day, there are men arrested and condemned, who regret what they have done. They are always ready to reimburse what they have stolen, but it is then too late. That is the principal laid down by the member for Jacques Cartier. But we cannot proceed by analogy. In the present case, there has been neither arrest nor conviction, and everything had been paid before a complaint had been laid against him. Not a day passes, in our ipolice courts, but that a denunciator complains of a transaction, and pretends that there has been fraud and false pretenses. What does then the magistrate? He does not deliver a writ of imprisonment. He has the accused brought before him. He asks him explanations, and if a discussion follows on the transaction the magistrate puts definitely the question and says to the individual:	There	has been a misunderstanding between you, you have obtained certain things under false pretenses, are you ready to return them? But certainly, will answer that individual. After that, could my learned friend get a writ against the one of whom he complains and who had no intention to steal. Never, and that is what occurs every day. Montreal is a large judiciary centre, the largest there is in our country. A great many denunciations and complaints are made there all the time. Not a week comes but justice has to intervene, and magistrates
deem it their duty to settle those disputes without arrest.
The member for Jacques Cartier has declared that Mr. Lanctot's house had been painted at too cheap a price. Where is the proof of that? On the contrary, have we not, in the evidence, the proof that the full and whole value of the work has been paid? That the amount paid by the member for Richelieu has been declared by disinterested men, and men knowing something about painting, to be fully sufficient to repay the government for what had been advanced, and more. But let us say that it was not more.
I have to call into question the affirmations of those gentlemen of the left. In order to be convinced, one must need have the truth of the facts. What we have to do here is to exercise our judgment and to appeal to our experience. Now, can we conclude, as has been said, that there was a theft. Not at all. We are ready for the fray, and we can keep it up with our friends of the left benches, because we are just as experienced as they are. The legal evidence which is submitted to us does not prove the accusations which have been brought. Indeed, after having heard the eloquent speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. Minister of Justice, no more doubts can subsist. Here is indeed a talented and superior man. He has shown that the independence of parliament had not been transgressed. He has shown that as clearly and peremptorily that two and two make four.
The hon. member for Terrebonne is not sufficiently versed in law to destroy that demonstration. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier would be the only one to try it, but without any hope of success.
I say that when those hon. gentlemen came to talk of malversation, of theft and of fraud, they are not serious. They have admitted that the one they wanted to reach was the hon. Minister of Marine. Here we can have an idea of the sincerity and frankness that the member for Terrebonne has put in that declaration.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has pretended that my friend of Richelieu has conspired. Let us suppose it is true. Well, Mr. Lanctot is guilty. But why has he conspired ? It has not been proved that there was a reward for him. Now, crime is always proceeded by a motive of gain, interest or profit which the criminal will derive or hopes to derive from his act. What was the interest of the member for Richelieu in conspiring ? Conspirators do not go into that game for pleasure, they never do Mr. Speaker.
The hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) has shown surprise at the accusation laid against him. He was real mad. Yet, that

was only a small matter. But, when it comes to others it is a considerable affair. He has been asked several times to tell what he knew about gasoline. That was not agreeable to him. He said he paid for what he had got, because he does not admit that he got anything from the government. He has even said : You accuse me wrongfully, and you are wrong in trying to pick that quarrel with me, because I have given to the government a value of nearly three thousand dollars. How generous of him to thus give three thousand dollars to a liberal government. How is any one to believe that he has ever given three thousand dollars for a railway in which he had no interest.
Here is indeed a man whose declaration may well be called into question. A man who is at war with the Minister of Marine, whom he accuses of graft and theft. He went even so far as saying to the Prime Minister : Be careful, do not call Mr. Bro-deur to the Supreme Court, that would be a disgrace.
As the hon. Minister of Justice has so well said, we are here the members sitting as judges in this cause. The preliminary inquiry, which goes on before the magistrate, has taken place before the committee. Five men have been charged to make the preliminary inquiry and to examine the facts. And when we see men having the merit of the members for Welland, Vercheres and Richmond, I say to the two others : You have talent and merit, but partisanship makes you see with eyes that are not the eyes of truth, and ail that because you cannot get the inquiry that you ask for. It is not fair to thus throw revenge on a member of this House, and all that because the government has not deemed expedient to grant them what they ask for.
The member for St. Anne has not dared to speak of the independence of parliament, and he had good reason for it. The member for St. Anne must have looked askance at all those who have spoken about independence, as for instance the member for Jacques Cartier.
* As has been said by the member for Vercheres, when that gentleman did judge convenient to leave the bench of magis-trature in order to sit here as a member of this House, he had the good sense to cast his vote in favour of drawing a pension of $4,300 a year as an ex-judge, and he has d'one well not to broach that subject. He was unwilling to speak about independence, because he was not without reproach in that respect.
Two weights and two measures, one for friends and the other for adversaries.
I have listened with attention to what the hon. member for Elgin West (Mr. Crothers) has said. He has exDressed himself without Mr. LAFORTTJNE.
the least gentleness and without caring in the least whom he might hurt. He had said to the House that this was a fraud and that there had been false pretenses. If he had opened any book upon criminal law or our own code, he would have seen what is meant by the word theft, and then he would not have spoken as he did. How can any man pretend that there have been false pretense when there is nothing to sustain an accusation of that kind.
He has quoted extracts of two papers which have taken our defence, and particm larly the Montreal 'Herald'. He has said that this was an important paper. I assert that the 'Hearld' has not then interpreted our sentiments. Besides, I must say that I have no fondness for a paper published by Mr. Walsh, who is always to be found in company with Mr. Henri Bourassa.
What about the 'Pays'?

That is another case of disappointment.
Mr. Walsh bestows praise on Mr. Henri Bourassa. He is there in bad company. The 'Herald' has not then -acted as a liberal newspaper should have done.
He has also quoted the Ottawa 'Free Press' What does that paper know about the evidence? What legal knowledge does he possess, that we might be prone to lay the opinion so luminously expressed by the hon. Minister of Justice. Here is a jurist whose life has -been -spent in the study of law. Could the publishers of those papers say the same thing? They may have acted in good faith, but I deny the legal authority of those papers. I say that they have not the necessary aptitudes nor the legal experience which would entitle them to throw blame on what has been done in the present case.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend was saying that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not approving that, the intention being here to have one believe that the Prime Minister was not in full agreement with his colleagues. It is a case of one can't have too much of a good thing. They ought to know that there are no traitors among us in the cabinet; that among us all are jointly and severally liable.
The hon. member for Elgin says all the contrary to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. He says that there has been- a conspiration. This is a new attack. He also sees false pretenses. There is not a word of that in the evidence. But those gentlemen, one after the other, have a new accusation to bring forward. If they were before a jury, I am sure they would not meet with much success. They would not get many convictions. We have heard about some malcontents. I remember so well what has occurred when the hon.

Minister of Marine was dismissing men in the employ of the government in Sorel. The next day, Conservative papers were denouncing him with violence. I will repeat here Iio-night to the hon. minister what I have told him elswhere. His mistake has been to tolerate too long old Conservatives who are there, playing knaves to the devil. If, on March 8, 1892, Honore Mercier has fallen from power, it was due to the traitors who were conspiring against him. I say then to the hon minister: Be firm, be just, but do not give to your adversaries an opportunity to overthrow you, that is tlheir function, and that is -what they will do on the first occasion.
The two gentlemen who have signed the minority report have no more merit, experience or honour than the three members of the sub-committee who have signed the other report. Why would we accept the minority report? Could those gentlemen have, by adventure, a monopoly of probity, merit and legal experience? They say that the evidence shows such and such a thing, and that the House is bound to accept that opinion. Their conduct does hot authorize us to believe that they are worth more than the others.
According to the hon. member for Terrebonne, there should be a general inquiry into the Sorel shipyards. If the government was appointing an impartial royal commissary, he would approve him. But, in order to have a commissary who would enjoy the confidence of those gentlemen of the left, it would be necessary, I suppose, to chose him in their ranks. If he was a liberal, they would criticise and paralyze him. The choice of a commissary would have to remain with them. Otherwise, he would be no good.
According to the hon. member for Terrebonne, Page and Champagne are frauds, and it follows naturally that my hon. friend of Richelieu must be guilty. What a nice way of reasoning! What a fine logic! If something could have been proven, it would be very different. But there is nothing in the evidence against Mr. Lanctot. according to the member for Terrebonne, Champagne and Page are thieves who have delivered goods from the Marine stores at Sorel to the member for Richelieu. It appears that they have had a dog-kennel built up, a cart painted, and a sewer-drain dug up.
How terrible, a dog-kennel! It appears that a cart has been painted. Just imagine such a scandal, coming after those of the Curran bridge, the Louise Basin and Me-Greevy. Those gentlemen of the left benches have so long lived among scandals that they see scandals everywhere. But those scandals were precisely the reason that made them lose the power. It was because
they had put under the ban of public opinion that they were forced to give up the power. They cry out to-day against scandals. They should keep quiet, because they could never find anything to equal what they have already done.
The hon. member for Terrebonne has admitted that, in themselves, those alleged scandals were insignificant, but that the question of principle was very important. Indeed they have principles. Their principle is to come back to power as soon as possible, but they will not see that day yet for a long time. And then we will see what their principles are. But we will denounce your principles.
It is very tedious to be in the opposition, when one is used to power, but those gentlemen of the left had better be comforted, because it will be at the very least 15 years before they get out of it. The public will be gracious to them only when the men he has been used to shall have disappeared and when others will have taken their place.
The member for Terrebonne has read a good many affidavits. It is an easy thing to get an affidavit ' ex-parte,' which is taken in the back-ground. But, Mr. Speaker, you cannot recall the past of any one without hearing what he has to say. The greatest criminals have the right to say to their accusers: Bring down your charges, meet me in a court of justice. But, ' ex-parte,' you could heap up lots of things against me which could not be accounted for. And why should we mention those things in this House, when they have been denied.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that I have answered categorically to those hon. gentlemen of the left.
I have not left anything without an answer. I noted carefully all that was said. I noticed in the first place their discrepancies, the lack of unanimity. People who are in the right necessarily agree ; truth by nature is simple and indivisible. So I note in the. first place their lack of agreement and of consistency ; their lack of sincerity. I have the proof of this in the last words of the member for Terrebonne ; it is not Mr. Lanctot who is guilty ; but if we are making such a fuss about the matter, it is because we were refused the investigation we asked for. The member for Richelieu will be exonerated of all wrongdoing; he will return home carrying his head high. But I say to these hon. gentlemen, have you the right to make of the good name and honour of your fellow-members a subject of laughter ? To-morrow, on meeting him, you will be the first to extend the hand of welcome.
I 'shall conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying to the member for Champlain, who is the immediate and direct cause of the wrong done to this man : You will never live old

enough to make up for this, and the responsibility of it all will rest on you. He will find out that the harm done to others is very often avenged on one's own family, and if he himself is not made to pay the debt, his own people will bear the burden of it ; for the responsibility he has assumed in respect to that family is enormous, he may never be in a position to liberate himself in this connection.
I shall leave the learned member with that to ponder over, and as for us we shall fulfil our duty.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) has claimed for himself the monopoly as it were of sincerity and patriotism. As to that he is greviously in error, and I for one shall undertake to look into this matter guided solely by the dictates of my conscience as a member of parliament and a citizen of Canada.
However, at this stage of the discussion, I cannot think of going over the whole ground once more and of making a thorough review of the facts connected with this unfortunate affair. I shall merely with the leave of the House, offer a few remarks and protest with all my might against the report of the majority of the committee on privileges and elections.
On March 6th, 1911, Mr. P. E. Blondin, member for Champlain, stated in the House of Commons that he had reason to believe that some varnishine and painting had been done by men in the employ, and with material the property of the Department of Marine at Sorel, for the benefit of Mr. A. Lanctot, member for Eichelieu. The charge was to the effect that, in the carrying out of such work, there had been wrong-doing, abuses, frauds, and embezzlement resorted to. It was charged that the hon. member for Eichelieu had unlawfully, in 1910, had men in the employ of the government to do work for his own benefit. Painting and painters' supplies, the property of the government, had been paid for out of the public funds of Canada, and the hon. member fox Eichelieu, it was stated, had profited thereby. The hon. member for Eichelieu asked for an investigation into such charges.
On that same day, the hon. member for Eichelieu acknowledged that, in the year 1910, he had had some painting done at his house by the men in the employ, and which supplies the property of the Department of Marine at Sorel; but that he had paid the salaries of the men and the cost of the supplies. There is one important point in respect to which the whole committee agreed; and it is this, that such work done for the benefit of a private citizen, was done outside the knowledge of the Department of Marine, of the superin-

tendent or deputy [DOT] superintendent of the yards at Sorel.
In thus endeavouring to protect the property of the government against one of his fellow-members and the men in the government's employ at Sorel, my hon. friend from Champlain has fulfilled a patriotic duty. He is entitled to the gratitude of the people for having thus endeavoured to do away with abuses which are a humiliation for parliament, degrade the dignity of parliament and tend to make fraud and embezzlement rampant among public servants.
The committee was entrusted with the task of determining in what measure the hon. member for Eichelieu, in his capacity of representative of the people, was affected by the charges and revelations of his colleague from Champlain.
The supporters of the government have not given expression to the slightest regret in connection with the wrong-doing, the abuses and the frauds, the existence of which nobody dares deny. They have got out a report which grievously pains those who are intent on doing away with the worst frauds committed in the handling of the people's money. Let us look into some of the facts.
It appears from the evidence that work was done at the house of the member for Eichelieu at the expense of the government and by men in the government's employ.
True, Mr. Lanctot refunded in November and December last the salaries paid to the painters and the cost of the supplies; but it is a crying abuse that a great public administration should be transformed into a.private undertaking for the benefit of a private citizen or a member of parliament. However, the majority of the committee have not a word of blame for the hon. gentleman from Eichelieu.
In the yards at Sorel, Mr. L. G. Papi-neau, superintendent, and Mr. H. A. Ter-reault, deputy superintendent, are exclusively empowered to order any work. The hon. member for Eichelieu acknowledges Mr. Papineau's powers; nevertheless, in Mr. Papineau's absence, he applies for men and supplies to officials in the employ of the government who are without authority and have not been empowered by their superior officers to comply with the wishes of the member for Eichelieu. The latter gentleman gets painters and supplies. Mr. Papineau spends the summer at Sorel, but Messrs. Lanctot, Page and Champagne, abstain, as guilty people, to apprise him of the work being carried on at Mr. Lanctot's house. In so doing was not Mr. Lanctot attempting to procure men and supplies outside the knowledge of the authorities.
If Mr. Lanctot was anxious to obtain men and supplies from Mr. Papineau, why did he apply to Mr. Page previous to March 29? Why did he call on Mr. Page previous

to calling on Mr. Papineau? Why did he not apply to Mr. Terreault, deputy superintendent? The hon. member for Richelieu is a barrister. He is acquainted with the law, and is aware that servants such as Messrs. Page and Champagne have no right to lend men or supplies the property of their employers without the knowledge and consent of the latter. Such action has brought about the falsifying of the pay lists for the Sorel yards, the falsifying of the accounts of the Department of Marine, and the infringement of all rules relative to the relations of chief and subaltern in the yards there. All of these transactions are clandestine. Why did Messrs. Lanctot, Page and Champagne go secretly about it? From June until November the people's money was used to pay for work done on behalf of the hon. member for Richelieu. What a sorry lesson of righteousness given to the people of Canada. Official publications do not supply us with any information enabling us to know with certainty that the amount reimbursed by Mr. Lanctot corresponds to that paid out on his account by the government. We have to rety on the word of men who falsified the pay lists. Is that satisfactory? However, the majority of the commission did not have a word of censure as regards the member for Richelieu. According to the report of the majority, Mr. Lanctot paid full value. On the other hand men have sworn that accounts had not been faithfully rendered to the Department of Marine. Thus, Alfred Douaire, painter is recorded as having worked only 18 days at the Lanctot house, while he swears he worked there for eight weeks. His evidence is supported by that of Henri Proulx and by that of Alfred Thi-baudeau. However, the majority of the committee entirely lose sight in their report of the evidence of that honest man. Questioned as to his reasons for having this work done by men in the employ of the government, Mr. Lanctot stated, among other things, the lack of available help. Now, the evidence shows that there was at the time, at Sorel, other painters which were not in the employ of the government and who would have been in a position to do the work at the house of the hon. member for Richelieu. Some of these painters even applied for the job, but were refused.
In answer to Mr. McDougall, Mr. Cartier, painter, stated: 'Mr. Lanctot came to me at the place where I was working-I was painting a house for Mr. Baril-and I applied for the job right there.'
Mr. Payette stated under oath that he was in a position to paint the house of the member for Richelieu. Such facts have no meaning in the minds of the hon. gentlemen making up the majority of the committee.
In 1910, Mr. Lussier, merchant at Sorel, got painters in the employ of the government and paid for them. Why did not the hon. gentleman follow the example of that citizen? In spite of evidence as to facts of the most grievous character, the majority state that the charges made by the hon. member for Champlain have not been supported. According to their report, Mr. Lanctot, in dealing with employees of the government which he supports, to his own advantage and to the detriment of the public, has not done anything contrary to the dignity of his office. What an example of dishonesty set out before the eyes of young Canadians !
That is a new easy-going principle enabling the servant to dispose of his master's property. Fortunately that obnoxious principle is condemned and repudiated by the newspaper men of the old liberal school.
I shall read the following extract from the majority report of the commission.
(Text.) Your committee feel in. view if tlie very serious nature of the charges made that they should express an opinion on the propriety of Mr. Blondin making the charges in the manner he did. Your committee do not wish to state that Mr. Blondin did not believe there was truth in the allegations, or that he did not act from a bona fide belief in their truthfulness, but the committee think that before making so serious a charge against an honourable member of the House of Commons, he should have made some independent inquiry to verify the truthfulness of the charges made and, which he apparently did not do. The Minister of Marine was called as a witness. His evidence as to this is on page 189 where he says he had information that no fraud had been committed and that all labour supplied by the shipyards had been paid for and all material supplied had been returned and which information he would have been pleased to give Mr. Blondin had he applied for same.	.
Your committee think that if Mr. Blondin had made these inquiries he would not and should not have made these charges,
(Translation.) My friend from Champlain has fulfilled his duty with prudence and enlightened patriotism. The member for Richelieu, the Minister of Marine and the Prime Minister of Canada had long been aware of the facts which were brought to the attention of the House on March 6. As far back as December 5, 1910, the hon. Minister of Marine had in his possession statements of a very important nature. At the time, men in the employ of the government were charging one another with thefts and graft. Cases of fraud and embezzlement were being ventilated. Why did not the hon. member for Richelieu and the hon. Minister of Marine make a clean breast of the whole matter previous to March 6?
How can the government newspapers and their supporters in this House decently cast aspersions on the hon. member for Champlain, when it is known that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, on January 18 wrote in the

following terms to a staunch liberal at Sorel, Mr. Albert Thibodeau?
Dear Sir,-In answer to your letter of the 16th instant, I have the honour to inform you that if any wrong doing has been carried on at Sorel, it is not the intention of the government to prevent such facts from being made public, on the contrary. Should there be any information in your possession, or in the possession of anybody else, as to what has been going on, the greatest latitude will be given you to make such facts known in the manner you think fit to do so.
Such words justify my hon. friend from Champlain.
Why did not the hon. Minister of Marine on March 6, show the lawfulness of the conduct of the member for Richelieu? Had he not at the time an exceptional opportunity for defending the hon. member? Let us be candid about it. The hon. minister entrusted with the honour and dignity of this department, was unwilling to take upon himself the responsibility of refusing an inquiry. He agreed to it. no doubt, as the best safeguard under the law against abuses and frauds. In granting this inquiry, he joined hands with us towards effecting a work of justice.
The supreme tribunal condemns with the utmost severity the men who favour by their silence administrative acts which smack of fraud and theft. We are called upon to pay taxes. However, the majority of the commission were not big enough to condemn abuses and show their gratitude towards the member for Champlain who has thrown light on a system of frauds bearing heavily on the country's finances. Their verdict does not contain even a gleam of hope for those who are anxious that grafting officials in the service of the State be done away with. They have only insults for a member who is unwilling to grant his protection to offenders against the common law. A little more, and the majority would have dubbed with some high sounding title the hon. member for Richelieu, together with Messrs. Page and Champagne. A little more and that majority would have branded as an unworthy citizen the member for Champlain who concerned himself with the interests of the Canadian people.
Important documents, solemn declarations were handed to my hon. friend from Champlain by respectable citizens. He would have betrayed his mandate by remaining silent, and the hon. member for Champlain is no traitor. The majority of the committee have whitewashed the hon. member for Richelieu. I refrain from congratulating them in this connection. At this very moment, independent newspaper men, whether Liberal or Conservative, unhesitatingly condemn the verdict of the majority of the commission. They refuse to cast aside the principle that public funds Mr. PAQUET.
should be applied exclusively to public ends.
Here is what I find in a good liberal paper, the ' Witness,' in its issue of April 7, 1911:
All the same, the evidence, though severely restricted, has been largely read, and people have formed their own opinion of government as carried on in Canada, and find it very hard to understand the exculpation given to the administration of the shipyard at Sorel. It is time the Marine Department was turned inside out. It is, we are repeatedly told, about to pass into the hands of a new chief, a man of action and in more robust health than Mr. Brodeur. If this be true, Mr. Lemieux has a task before him that will make or mar him.
(Translation.) Then we have ' La Patrie ' of April 6, 1911:
Now, government supporters, who necessarily have the upper end whenever the committee come to a decision, after conscientiously looking into the facts, which in any case are undeniable, pronounced this judgment, which will remain as a monument, in the history of this country:
(1)	Mr. Lanctot is exonerated from all blame.
(2)	There is no exception to be taken to the system in vogue in the shipyards at Sorel, to lend to all comers men and material which are government property and paid for out of public funds.
(3)	One thing only should be condemned; that is the charge brought forward against Mr. Lanotot; one man only should be frowned upon, that is Mr. Blondin whom the majority of the committee condemn most severely.
We believe that the parliament buildings never before witnessed such a farce.
On April 20, the * Herald,' unable to control any longer its indignation expressed itself as follows in an editorial entitled ' The shoe on the wrong foot.'
(Text.) He seems to be content to prove that he paid for the painters' time and replaced the materials used on his place. He does seem to recognize that it was unworthy of him as a member of parliament to arrange with subordinate officials, without the knowledge of their superiors on the spot, even, to have men working for him whose services were all the time being charged to the Crown and presumably apportioned against some work that had been ordered by parliament. If Mr. Lanctot cannot see the unworthiness of that, he ought to be in some other role than that of a Liberal party leader. Certainly no government, Liberal or other, can be maintained in this country on the principle that its supporters in parliament are justified in such enterprises.
(Translation.) It is generally known that the ' Herald,' the largest English liberal organ in the metropolis of Canada, is the organ of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. The latter gentleman is aware that I have towards him feelings of great respect, on account of his honesty and his

untiring industry. He cannot doubt of my sincerity.
According to ' La Patrie ' that editorial of the ' Herald ' has caused a profound sensation. It is the legitimate and undisguised condemnation of the conduct of the hon. member for Richelieu.
It is interesting to read the following extracts from ' La Patrie,' of April 21:
It is an objectionable means of forwarding the interests of a party to approve doings of its members which the law and mere common sense show to be worthy of condemnation.
If the Committe on Privileges and Elections had, while granting to Mr. Lanctot the benefit of attenuating circumstances, condemned the abuses which the investigation clearly showed to have been committed, public opinion might have approved their stand.
But by obstinately closing their eyes to abuses, by even giving evidence of boldness and stupidity to the point of censuring Mr. Blondin for having drawn the attention of the House and the country to such facts, the majority of the committee have discredited themselves in the eyes of the country at large, and merited the condemnation even of liberal members.
I shall quote further an extract from the organ of the liberal party in this city. The ' Free Press ' published the following on April 25:
(Text.) But what be should have done the moment the charge was preferred against him was to have resigned his seat and appealed to his constituents for re-election. He could then have been re-elected by acclamation; whether he could do so now is another question.
Where a member of a party in the control of the public business places himself, wittingly or nnwittingly, under the penalties of the parliament Act there is only one course open for him to take, and that is what Mr. Lanctot should have done.
For him to now ask a majority of the House -of Commons to excuse his fault is to ask many of them to cancel their own records, and we do not believe that they will do so.
If Mr. Lanctot has committed a breach of the parliament Act, his is the offence.
Why should the Liberal party as a whole accept any share of his blame?
(Translation.) I am glad to say so, Liberal papers give evidence of a spirit of fairness which overrides the judgment of the majority of the Committee on Privileges and Elections.
Conservative members of the committee aforesaid did not wait for the expression of such feelings of indignation to condemn the hon. member for Richelieu. They have assumed a patriotic duty and risen above mere considerations of friendship to condemn the deed's- of Mr. Lanctot. I heartily approve of the report of the minority, and, if the House will allow me, I shall read the conclusions of that judgment which will surely be sanctioned by public opinion:
(Text.) It is our conclusion from the [DOT]evidence that Mr. Adelard Lanctot, a member
of the House of Commons, knowingly and unlawfully did procure the employees of the government of Canada to do certain work for him and on his behalf in the year 1910, he then being a member of the said House, and by collusion with the servants of the government did procure the payment of such labour by and out of the public moneys of the Dominion of Canada for his own purposes and benefit, without lawful right and contrary to the public interest. ,
That he did furthermore, knowingly and unlawfully, cause and procure certain materials, the property of the government of Canada to he delivered to himself for his own benefit and use, he then being a member of the House of Commons, and with such intent and purpose did collude and contrive with the servants of the Dominion of Canada to whom the said materials had been entrusted for use in the works of said government to so deliver the same to him by unlawful misappropriation, contrary to their duty and obligation to the government and contrary to law and the public interest.
And further it is our conclusion that the said Adelard Lanctot, by the acts and proceedings aforesaid, did infringe the independence of parliament.
(Translation.) That investigation of a decidely narrow scope has brought to light what is possibly a mere sample incident in the management of the government yards at Soiel.
Is not the government property in that city in the hands of officials unworthy of the confidence of the Canadian people? There public servants have transgressed the most commonplace notions of equity. Their moral responsibility is not so great if they are the unfortunate victims of that political pressure -which bears as heavily as lead on the shoulders of all throughout our province.
The hon. Minister of Marine confines building materials, goods and the management of -men in his department to the care of officials who have falsified entries in the public records. And if the House, approving of the principles of the majority of the committee, refrains from condemning the abuses found rampant at Sorel, and- censures the patriot anxious to cut out the diseased parts, then, will not these officials commit to-morrow deeds still more obnoxious.
According to the solemn declaration of Mr. D. Peloquin, several men in the -employ of the government at Sorel, charge one another with stealing cement, timber, iron, paint and particularly the time of government men who are sent out to do work for private parties while drawing pay from the government. Within the last two years, the government must have lost at Sorel more than $50,000 on account of frauds and thefts.
It would- be an easy matter to obtain numerous statements giving evidence of

graft and thefts at Sorel. As stated in 'La Patrie'.
Public rumour points to a large number of schemes still unrevealed, whereby building materials and other goods belonging to the shipyards have become the-property of private parties without the government being paid for them. Following on the evidence taken under oath, it is imperative that a thorough investigation should be made into the inside management of the yards at Sorel. It is a matter of doing away with thefts, and the voice of consicence should just now be heard in preference to that of the petty interests of political factions.
I attach the greatest importance to these remarks of 'La Patrie'.
The Minister of Marine cannot hope to appease the fears and suspicions of the people by entrusting officials of his department with the task of carrying on an investigation in this connection. Our national life suffers from abuses, thefts and dishonesty in the handling of public funds.
The government should appoint a Royal Commission to thoroughly overhaul the management of the Sorel yards. Confidence in the Department of Marine should be restored by finding out who are the wrongdoers and punishing them for their crimes. But let us not strike the men who aTe courageous enough to point out abuses and thefts. It is not a secret inquiry I am asking for, but rather a public investigation, for publicity is the terror of criminals.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be
brief, not wishing at this late hour of the night to give my opponents an opportunity of charging me with a further offence, that of prolonging the debate. I regret that the right hon. Prime Minister should not be in his place, as I would have liked to put to him a question which can properly be answered only by himself ; and I cannot refrain from expressing my surprise at the indifference shown by the right hon. gentleman in respect to this debate ; I wonder whether pangs of conscience have not tardily induced him to abstain from playing a part in the criminal farce which is going on here just now.
The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries is bold enough to insinuate that I should have made inquiries from him before making these charges. To this my answer will be very brief. He was in the House when I made my charges. Since he had in hand, according to his contention, the proofs of the innocence of the member for Richelieu, why did he not then rise in his seat and make known these proofs? I would have "withdrawn my charges and an investigation would not have been required.
But Mr. Speaker, that contention of the Mr. PAQTTET.
minister's ia merely blundering and trickery on his part. The evidence has shown that, even had the minister been willing in good faith to carry on with me a private inquiry, he would not have discovered anything ; for they had been very careful to cover up all their tracks, and the books which we might have looked into would not have supplied any information, for they were falsified. I challenge the minister to contradict me when I say that even at the present time he is not in a position to carry on a thorough investigation, tihe documents having been destroyed and the books falsified.
I realize that I am not to discuss the evidence, the facts, or the report of the committee in this case wherein I stand as one of the parties, but I wish to protest with all my might against that part af the majority report which reflects on me personally, and attempts to make me play the part of the guilty party in connection with this inquiry.
The political bias of the hon. gentlemen supporting the government, their blind and vicious partisanship has prevented them from seeing for themselves the stupidity of the course they took in an effort to show me in a bad light ; but public opinion voiced in the newspapers throughout the country, to whatever party they belong, and even in some of the most influential of the liberal organs, has finally recalled these hon. gentlemen to a sense of decency and caused them to pass silently over that shameful paTt of their report.
This eveniug not a single one of them dared to make reference to that part of the report; they remained silent as they are all ashamed of it, and have heard the whole country condemning them; and these same gentlemen who yesterday were threatening to eject and lynch me, have no longer a single word of condemnation, and stupidly keep their mouths closed while I throw out to them from my seat the expression of my contempt.
The supporters of the government have exerted all their efforts, their eloquence and their intellectual resources, to throw a red herring across the trail, with a view to inspiring sympathy on behalf for the member for Richelieu, and restricting this whole debate to a petty question of dollars and cents. But they will not succeed in misleading the honest common sense of the Canadian people; they will not mislead this clear-minded, far-seeing and honest judge, who, long before the ridiculous attempt of to-night, severely condemned the member, the department and the methods which I denounced. Let these hon. gentlemen opposite make up their minds that this question by far surpasses all of them, from the smallest to the greatest; it implies the most important of our principles of government.

that of the integrity of parliament and the honour of the nation. That is the true scope of this debate; and it cannot be reduced a single inch.
Let those who listen to me and stare at me from the government side, listen to this: I have for Mr. Lanctot all the sympathy and all the regard which a member of this House owes to a fellow-member; I have for hon. gentlemen on the other side, as well as on this side, all the respect which they are entitled to, but let me say one thing: whenever that sympathy conflicts with my bounden duty, I shall not hesitate for one moment to sacrifice it and trample it under foot; and whenever they stand between me and the fulfilment of my public duties, as well as the dictates of honesty and of my conscience, they may rest assured that I shall run them down without any compunction.
And if they will allow me to repeat it, it is not here a matter of discussing Mr. Lanctot, or the Liberal party or anybody else in this House, but solely the good management of public affairs and the honour of the nation.
An hon. member who has to do with criminal matters in the district of Montreal, the member for Montcalm (Mr. La-fortune), has attempted to play on the emotions of hon. members, in the midst of the stupid things making up his farcical speech; he hurled at me maledictions, omens of ill, as an old-time sorcerer might have done, and called on me to make amends for the tears for the shedding of which I am to be held responsible. He forgot for a moment-an unusual occurrence-the position he is entrusted with. Appearing from day to day, as he does, before the criminal courts, on behalf of the Crown, to have all offenders punished, what would he answer were I to ask him to make amends for all the sorrows he thus causes from day to day, he who is constantly arguing for the imposition of penalties, corporal punishments and even the capital punishment.
Now, I am aware that the right hon. Prime Minister will be here shortly and that he will vote in favour of the motion to w'hitewash the member for Richelieu. May I request of him to state to the country if, in so voting, he means to condone in every respect the conduct of the member for Richelieu, and whether he intends to inform by to-morrow the thousands of public servants, the representatives of the people, the public men who will read the report of this debate, and whether he wishes to have it repeated in all the homes and families throughout the country, that it is a lawful thing to embezzle the public funds and property for the benefit of individuals, and whether he is ready to throw the august mantle of the Prime Minister of Canada to cover up such wrong-doing, provided the
moneys which have been taken are subsequently returned?
